variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is a way to tune a model toward responses people judge as better. A team asks people to compare candidate responses, trains a reward model to predict those preferences, then updates a policy to earn more predicted reward.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “How does an RLHF system turn feedback into a release?”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Start from SFT
pairs.detail: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains on high-quality demonstrations so the policy can already follow instructions before preference optimization begins.
pairs.explanation: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains on high-quality demonstrations so the policy can already follow instructions before preference optimization begins.

pairs.label: Collect preferences
pairs.detail: Show comparable candidate responses under a rubric, randomize presentation, record disagreement, and preserve prompt, annotator, and policy-version metadata.
pairs.explanation: Show comparable candidate responses under a rubric, randomize presentation, record disagreement, and preserve prompt, annotator, and policy-version metadata.

pairs.label: Fit a reward model
pairs.detail: Train a scalar scorer to rank chosen responses above rejected responses, then test it on held-out prompts and important slices.
pairs.explanation: Train a scalar scorer to rank chosen responses above rejected responses, then test it on held-out prompts and important slices.

pairs.label: Update conservatively
pairs.detail: Use rollouts and the reward model to improve the policy while penalizing divergence from a frozen reference policy.
pairs.explanation: Use rollouts and the reward model to improve the policy while penalizing divergence from a frozen reference policy.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Optimization quality is bounded by preference-data validity, reward-model generalization, and constrained policy updates.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Start from SFT: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains on high-quality demonstrations so the policy can already follow instructions before preference optimization begins. Collect preferences: Show comparable candidate responses under a rubric, randomize presentation, record disagreement, and preserve prompt, annotator, and policy-version metadata. Fit a reward model: Train a scalar scorer to rank chosen responses above rejected responses, then test it on held-out prompts and important slices. Update conservatively: Use rollouts and the reward model to improve the policy while penalizing divergence from a frozen reference policy.

variants.title: Make the decision
variants.context: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is a way to tune a model toward responses people judge as better. A team asks people to compare candidate responses, trains a reward model to predict those preferences, then updates a policy to earn more predicted reward.
variants.prompt: What does a reward model learn from a chosen and rejected response for the same prompt?
options: A score that should rank the chosen response above the rejected response
A deterministic proof that the chosen response is safe
The tokenizer vocabulary for both responses
The policy's future KL target
variants.explanation: Pairwise reward modeling learns a preference-ranking proxy. It is evidence about observed comparisons, not a proof of intent or safety.

variants.prompt: A reward model has strong average held-out accuracy but poor coverage for a high-risk language slice. What is the best next step?
options: Collect and evaluate representative comparisons for that slice before broad policy optimization
Increase PPO epochs until average reward rises
Remove the slice from release evaluation
Treat the average score as sufficient evidence
variants.explanation: Average accuracy can hide an important failure slice. The missing evidence should be collected and evaluated before optimization expands the behavior.

variants.prompt: What is a key trade-off of DPO relative to a PPO-style RLHF loop?
options: DPO can avoid a separate reward model and online rollouts, but it still depends on valid preference data
DPO makes preference data unnecessary
DPO proves that a model cannot exploit a proxy
DPO always requires more policy rollouts than PPO
variants.explanation: DPO simplifies the optimization setup by learning directly from preference pairs, but it cannot fix biased, incomplete, or unrepresentative preferences.

variants.prompt: Why does RLHF penalize KL divergence from a frozen reference policy?
options: To limit movement toward response regions where the reward model and regression suite have less evidence
To guarantee the policy is aligned with every user
To remove the need for an independent evaluation set
To make annotation free
variants.explanation: A KL penalty is a trust-region-style brake. It limits policy movement but does not validate the reward model or replace external evaluation.

variants.prompt: Why should an RLHF release use evaluators that were not optimized directly by the reward model?
options: They can reveal proxy blind spots, capability regressions, and safety failures
They make KL divergence exactly zero
They eliminate the need to version data
They replace monitoring after release
variants.explanation: Independent evaluation provides evidence outside the reward model's objective and must continue into staged release monitoring.
